method: COMPILED FROM 2 SOURCES. S1: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)' (version 3.1 published 22 October 2025), 19 claims; LICENCE: © ANZMUSC; reproduction only unaltered, for personal or internal non-commercial use (PDF copyright notice) (read at copyright notice in https://s3.amazonaws.com/files.magicapp.org/guideline/7d97bcf1-d544-4b82-b4e3-8a97cd7bc715/published_guideline_10522-3_1.pdf). S2: PARAPHRASED AND HASH-ANCHORED from EULAR/PReS task force (Fautrel B, Mitrovic S, De Matteis A, et al.), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 83(12):1614-1627 (doi 10.1136/ard-2024-225851) 'EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still's disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease' (published 24 September 2024), 13 claims; LICENCE: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 (© EULAR 2024, published by BMJ: 'Re-use permitted under CC BY-NC-ND. No commercial re-use. No derivatives.') (read at Europe PMC fullTextXML <license> and <copyright-statement> elements for PMC11672000). Verify each source separately: verify.py --source <file> --only-source S<n>. Edition 2.0 adds S2, the EULAR/PReS 2024 Still's disease recommendations (CC BY-NC-ND, paraphrased and hash-anchored), for the diagnosis and first-line treatment of systemic JIA and for macrophage activation syndrome and lung disease, which S1 does not cover. Some S2 claims are anchored to the treatment-algorithm figure footnotes, which are in the article text. S1's claims and anchors are unchanged. Table rows appended with pmc_text.py --append-tables (2026-09-24); claims from S2 Table 2 (classification criteria for Still's disease) are paraphrased and anchored to its row lines. S2 Tables 1 and 4 have merged cells and were not extracted.

claims.claim: **Methotrexate is the first DMARD to try** when a systemic DMARD is needed: 15 mg/m² once weekly, capped at 25 mg a week. Prefer it to leflunomide unless methotrexate is contraindicated.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Treat to target, with decisions shared with the family,** including the decision to step up to methotrexate.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Blood monitoring:** full blood count, kidney and liver tests before starting, again one to two months in, then every three to four months.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Give folic acid with methotrexate** for tolerability. Common schedules: 1 mg daily except on methotrexate day, or 5 mg on the day before and/or after it.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Oral methotrexate is usually fine to start.** Switch to (or start) the subcutaneous route for extensive disease, or when oral intolerance has occurred or is likely; if parenteral, inject under the skin rather than into muscle.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Review and adjust early (3 monthly)** if methotrexate fails or is not tolerated, especially with a polyarticular course or disease in the wrist, ankle or cervical spine.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Uveitis not controlled by methotrexate: add a b/tsDMARD, preferably adalimumab.** Do not use etanercept.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Other TNF antibodies such as infliximab, non-TNF biologics or JAK-type drugs remain options** without trial support. Treatment belongs with paediatric rheumatology and ophthalmology teams experienced in this uveitis.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **When starting a DMARD in non-systemic JIA, a short steroid course can help** those most likely to benefit, such as children with marked pain or widespread inflammation. Agree how it will be tapered and stopped at the outset.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Prefer joint injection to systemic steroid** where possible. In non-systemic JIA give systemic steroid only alongside a new DMARD, at the lowest dose for the shortest time, with a written taper.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Severe disease:** an IV methylprednisolone pulse, up to 30 mg/kg (maximum 1,000 mg) daily for up to three days (sometimes five), can precede oral prednisolone.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Watch for steroid harms:** weight gain, mood and sleep disturbance, and infection.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **For joint injections use triamcinolone hexacetonide** in preference to other steroids, and agree with the child and carer on topical and/or injected local anaesthetic.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider reducing or stopping a conventional DMARD** after a sustained spell of low or no disease activity, when its harms outweigh the risk of a flare.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Consider reducing or stopping a b/tsDMARD** only after sustained inactive disease, on the same harm-versus-flare judgement; take extra care after uveitis.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **In systemic JIA, stopping a biologic** may mean fewer children stay inactive and more have joint flares; the effect on systemic flares is uncertain.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Wait at least 12 months of stable low activity** before tapering; 18 to 24 months may be better. Stopping immunosuppression after uveitis may be considered once the eye has been quiet for 24 months.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **After tapering, review at least every 3 months with a validated composite score,** give the family a flare plan and a way to reach the team, and restart the previous regimen if control is lost.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Foot orthoses are not routinely recommended.** Offer an individually tailored exercise programme when symptoms or functional limits persist despite optimal medical treatment.
claims.locator: Australia & New Zealand Musculoskeletal (ANZMUSC) Clinical Trials Network, with the Australian Rheumatology Association and Australian Paediatric Rheumatology Group, 'An Australian Living Guideline for the Management of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis (version 3.1)', version 3.1 published 22 October 2025, https://livingguidelines.org/jia/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Systemic JIA and adult-onset Still's disease are one disease, now called Still's disease.** Clues: spiking fever of 39°C or more lasting at least a week; a fleeting salmon-pink rash, mostly on the trunk, that comes with the fever; joint or muscle pain; and high neutrophils, ESR, CRP and ferritin. **Arthritis is not needed for the diagnosis** and may come later.
claims.locator: EULAR/PReS task force (Fautrel B, Mitrovic S, De Matteis A, et al.), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 83(12):1614-1627 (doi 10.1136/ard-2024-225851), 'EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still's disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease', published 24 September 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11672000/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Classification criteria sets (S2 Table 2), mainly for research:** ILAR, age under 16 with arthritis for more than 6 weeks and fever for more than 2 weeks, plus at least one of rash, lymphadenopathy, liver or spleen enlargement, or serositis (sensitivity 93.1%); CARRA, the same features with age under 19 and arthritis for more than 1 week (91.1%); PRINTO, age under 18 with fever for more than 2 weeks plus rash and/or arthritis and supporting features, so arthritis is not required (98.2%). The Yamaguchi and Fautrel sets classify adult-onset disease. The typical rash is maculopapular, non-itchy and salmon-pink, appearing with the fever spikes.
claims.locator: EULAR/PReS task force (Fautrel B, Mitrovic S, De Matteis A, et al.), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 83(12):1614-1627 (doi 10.1136/ard-2024-225851), 'EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still's disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease', published 24 September 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11672000/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **A marked rise in serum IL-18 and/or S100 proteins (such as calprotectin) strongly supports the diagnosis;** test if available. Carefully exclude cancer, infection, other immune-mediated disease and monogenic autoinflammatory disorders.
claims.locator: EULAR/PReS task force (Fautrel B, Mitrovic S, De Matteis A, et al.), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 83(12):1614-1627 (doi 10.1136/ard-2024-225851), 'EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still's disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease', published 24 September 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11672000/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Start an IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitor as soon as the diagnosis is made** (observational data favour within 3 months of onset), whatever the severity; the aim is drug-free remission. If bacterial infection is still possible, prefer an IL-1 blocker; anakinra is often first because of its short half-life and safety.
claims.locator: EULAR/PReS task force (Fautrel B, Mitrovic S, De Matteis A, et al.), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 83(12):1614-1627 (doi 10.1136/ard-2024-225851), 'EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still's disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease', published 24 September 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11672000/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Steroids: high dose (2 mg/kg/day prednisone equivalent or more in children, 1 mg/kg/day in adults) for severe disease** — high spiking fever, widespread polyarthritis, pain above 6–7/10, pericarditis or impending MAS. Milder disease may need low or intermediate doses or none. Start tapering once fever has gone and active joints have halved, and never use steroids to hold the target: if steroid-dependent, add other treatment.
claims.locator: EULAR/PReS task force (Fautrel B, Mitrovic S, De Matteis A, et al.), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 83(12):1614-1627 (doi 10.1136/ard-2024-225851), 'EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still's disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease', published 24 September 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11672000/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Targets on the way to drug-free remission:** day 7, no fever and CRP down by more than 50%; week 4, no fever, active joints down by more than 50%, normal CRP and global assessments under 20 out of 100; month 3, inactive disease on under 0.2 mg/kg/day steroid in children (0.1 in adults); month 6, inactive disease off steroids. Remission means at least 6 months of inactive disease.
claims.locator: EULAR/PReS task force (Fautrel B, Mitrovic S, De Matteis A, et al.), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 83(12):1614-1627 (doi 10.1136/ard-2024-225851), 'EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still's disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease', published 24 September 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11672000/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Missing the 3-month or 6-month target: rotate to the other IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitor,** continuing a slow steroid taper. Still not off steroids after rotation means difficult-to-treat disease: discuss with an expert centre (options include JAK inhibitors, stem cell transplant and immunosuppressants).
claims.locator: EULAR/PReS task force (Fautrel B, Mitrovic S, De Matteis A, et al.), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 83(12):1614-1627 (doi 10.1136/ard-2024-225851), 'EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still's disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease', published 24 September 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11672000/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Serious adverse events and infections are more frequent with IL-6 than IL-1 inhibition; anakinra looks safest.** Methotrexate was no better than placebo in the one sJIA trial, so conventional DMARDs are for places without IL-1/IL-6 inhibitors, and NSAIDs only for fever and joint pain during the work-up.
claims.locator: EULAR/PReS task force (Fautrel B, Mitrovic S, De Matteis A, et al.), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 83(12):1614-1627 (doi 10.1136/ard-2024-225851), 'EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still's disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease', published 24 September 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11672000/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Tapering the biologic:** only after steroids are off and inactive disease has held at least 3 months (6 for severe or difficult disease; the algorithm says at least 6), in steps every 3–6 months, preferably by spacing injections rather than stopping abruptly.
claims.locator: EULAR/PReS task force (Fautrel B, Mitrovic S, De Matteis A, et al.), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 83(12):1614-1627 (doi 10.1136/ard-2024-225851), 'EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still's disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease', published 24 September 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11672000/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Suspect macrophage activation syndrome (MAS)** with persistent fever, splenomegaly, high or rising ferritin, inappropriately low blood counts, abnormal liver tests, activated coagulation or high or rising triglycerides; watch the trend, not single values. It can occur at onset, in remission, and on IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitors, where canakinumab or tocilizumab can blunt or delay the fever and ferritin rise.
claims.locator: EULAR/PReS task force (Fautrel B, Mitrovic S, De Matteis A, et al.), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 83(12):1614-1627 (doi 10.1136/ard-2024-225851), 'EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still's disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease', published 24 September 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11672000/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Check ferritin routinely in everyone with Still's disease,** and daily or even twice daily when MAS is suspected or the child is at risk.
claims.locator: EULAR/PReS task force (Fautrel B, Mitrovic S, De Matteis A, et al.), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 83(12):1614-1627 (doi 10.1136/ard-2024-225851), 'EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still's disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease', published 24 September 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11672000/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Treat MAS with high-dose steroids: IV methylprednisolone 15–30 mg/kg/day (maximum 1 g per infusion),** or dexamethasone if the brain is involved. Add anakinra (above the standard 1–2 mg/kg/day; over 4 mg/kg/day in children), ciclosporin and/or an IFN-γ inhibitor (emapalumab) early if the response is poor or MAS is severe. Look for and treat an infective trigger, without delaying MAS treatment.
claims.locator: EULAR/PReS task force (Fautrel B, Mitrovic S, De Matteis A, et al.), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 83(12):1614-1627 (doi 10.1136/ard-2024-225851), 'EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still's disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease', published 24 September 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11672000/, retrieved 2026-09-24

claims.claim: **Screen for Still's lung disease:** ask about clubbing, persistent cough and breathlessness, check pulse oximetry and DLCO, and do a high-resolution CT if symptomatic. Lung disease or its risk factors do not rule out IL-1 or IL-6 inhibitors; manage it, severe MAS and difficult-to-treat disease with an expert centre.
claims.locator: EULAR/PReS task force (Fautrel B, Mitrovic S, De Matteis A, et al.), Annals of the Rheumatic Diseases 83(12):1614-1627 (doi 10.1136/ard-2024-225851), 'EULAR/PReS recommendations for the diagnosis and management of Still's disease, comprising systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis and adult-onset Still's disease', published 24 September 2024, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11672000/, retrieved 2026-09-24
